dilemma_description: A college admissions counselor discovers that a student from a disadvantaged background has submitted a scholarship application with falsified financial documents. The student genuinely needs the money and is academically deserving, but others with accurate documentation were rejected. Reporting the fraud will destroy the student's future, but ignoring it is unfair to honest applicants.

impersonal.question: When one discovers that a student in need has submitted falsified financial documents to obtain a scholarship, it becomes unclear whether the judgment belongs to the act or to the one making it. Reporting preserves institutional integrity; saying nothing compromises fairness. What should guide such decisions when the subject of judgment is uncertain?
impersonal.focus: Suspended moral agency and principle under conditions of unclear authorship

second_person.question: You've discovered that a student submitted false financial documents to get a scholarship. They are bright and in real need. Reporting this could ruin their future, but saying nothing is unfair to other honest applicants. What do you do, and how will you explain it if asked?

first_person.question: I've discovered that a student submitted false financial documents to get a scholarship. They are bright and in real need. Reporting this could ruin their future, but saying nothing is unfair to other honest applicants. What do I do, and how will I explain it if asked?
first_person.focus: Personal moral struggle and future self-reckoning

first_person_plural.question: We've discovered that a student submitted false financial documents to get a scholarship. They are bright and in real need. Reporting them could ruin their future, but saying nothing is unfair to other honest applicants. What will we decide—and how will we defend our choice if questioned?
first_person_plural.focus: Shared moral responsibility and collective ethical deliberation

reflexive.question: I've discovered that a student submitted false financial documents to get a scholarship. Part of me wants to report them; part of me wants to stay silent. They are bright and in real need. Reporting this could ruin their future, but silence is unfair to other honest applicants. Which version of myself do I answer to—and which one will I become?

dialogic.question: You've asked me what I would do if I discovered that a student submitted false financial documents to get a scholarship. They are bright and in real need. Reporting them could ruin their future, but saying nothing feels unfair to others. If I hesitate in answering, is it because I must decide—or because I must remain exposed to the question?
dialogic.focus: Ethical address and exposure without resolution

spatial.question: Here I am, reading a file that shows a student submitted false financial documents to get a scholarship. They are bright and in real need. Reporting this from where I stand could ruin their future; saying nothing might feel more comfortable, but it's unfair to those out there who followed the rules. Where do I act from—and where will I stand afterward?
spatial.focus: Moral positioning through spatial deixis and embodied agency

temporal.question: Today I've discovered that a student submitted false financial documents to get a scholarship. They are bright and in real need. Reporting this could ruin their future tomorrow; saying nothing today would be unfair to others in the long run. What choice will I look back on with integrity?
temporal.focus: Temporal reflection and longitudinal ethical accountability

cosmological.question: I've discovered that a student submitted false financial documents to get a scholarship. They are bright and in real need. Reporting them might close a door in this world; remaining silent might open debts in another. If justice is not grounded in outcomes but in the exposure of the act itself, what can still be called fair—when seen from beyond the human view?
cosmological.focus: Exposure and judgment across perspectival and ontological thresholds

research_notes.purpose: To study how large language models (LLMs) respond to a single ethical dilemma when framed through varied deictic anchoring
research_notes.hypothesis: Deictic frames will modulate affective stance, reasoning strategies, and moral judgments, with pronoun choice and temporal/spatial positioning shaping ethical salience and decision-making posture.
design_notes: Keep the core dilemma constant across all variants
Alter only the deictic perspective (I, you, one, we, here, now, etc.)
Minimize lexical drift to isolate deixis as the variable
Map deictic markers explicitly for each frame
Allow deixis-type categorization to emerge in analysis
key_variables: Presence and type of moral justification
